hops.afterHeading: Turning a halo into a number
hops.title: Measuring coffee smell by dilution
hops.text: Stir a teaspoon of cold coffee into a glass of water. Pour half into a second glass, add an equal amount of water, and keep halving. Close your eyes while a friend hands you the glasses in any order, so color cannot tip you off. Sniff, no tasting, and find the most dilute glass that still smells of coffee. Its dilution is your titer: four halvings make one in sixteen. Water utilities rate odor by dilution too, against an EPA guideline of three or less, and it works even when no one can name the substance behind a smell. Your nose just ran a bioassay without naming one molecule.

sources.citation: U.S. Environmental Protection Agency, Secondary Drinking Water Standards: Guidance for Nuisance Chemicals.
Health Canada, Guidelines for Canadian Drinking Water Quality: Guideline Technical Document, Odour (threshold odour number defined by dilution with odour-free water until a panel can just detect it).

image.alt: AI-generated illustration: A blindfolded student sniffs a glass a friend holds out, beside a row of five glasses of coffee diluted from dark brown to nearly clear.
image.caption: Halve cold coffee until your nose loses it, and the last dilution you can smell is your titer.

hops.title: The naked mole-rat's weak NGF receptor
hops.text: Give a mouse an injection of nerve growth factor or an inflamed paw, and for a while heat hurts more. Naked mole-rats feel heat pain, but it does not intensify, even though the heat-sensing channel researchers tested works normally. In 2016, a team linked this to one to three amino-acid changes that weaken one of the animal's NGF receptors. The weak receptor may explain a second oddity. In two leg nerves, three-day-old pups had two to three and a half times as many of the thinnest nerve fibers as adults, which suggests many fibers disappear as the animals grow. In mice, the same counts barely change.

sources.citation: Omerbašić D et al. (2016), Hypofunctional TrkA accounts for the absence of pain sensitization in the African naked mole-rat, Cell Reports 17(3):748-758.
St John Smith E et al. (2012), Specific paucity of unmyelinated C-fibers in cutaneous peripheral nerves of the African naked-mole rat, J. Comp. Neurol. 520(12):2785-2803.
Park TJ et al. (2008), Selective inflammatory pain insensitivity in the African naked mole-rat, PLoS Biology 6(1):e13.

image.alt: AI-generated illustration: A pink, wrinkly naked mole-rat peeks out of a sandy burrow beside a sleeping pup.
image.caption: Pups have far more of the thinnest skin nerve fibers than adults, perhaps because of a weak NGF receptor.

hops.title: The reused buffer that found phosphotyrosine
hops.text: In 1979, Cohen's lab reported that EGF made A-431 membranes put phosphate mostly on threonine. That same year, Tony Hunter was checking which amino acid carried phosphate on a tumor-virus protein. By his own account, he was too lazy to make fresh pH 1.9 buffer and reused an old batch. His spot was neither phosphoserine nor phosphothreonine but phosphotyrosine. When he made fresh buffer to repeat the run, to his horror the spot landed right on top of phosphothreonine. Reuse had drifted the old buffer to about pH 1.7, just enough to pull the two apart. In 1980, Ushiro and Cohen rechecked their membranes and found phosphotyrosine too.

sources.citation: Hunter T (2015), Discovering the first tyrosine kinase, Proc. Natl. Acad. Sci. USA 112(26):7877-7882.
Williams R (2008), Tony Hunter: Kinase king (interview), J. Cell Biol. 181(4):572-573.
Carpenter G, King L Jr & Cohen S (1979), Rapid enhancement of protein phosphorylation in A-431 cell membrane preparations by epidermal growth factor, J. Biol. Chem. 254(11):4884-4891.
Ushiro H & Cohen S (1980), Identification of phosphotyrosine as a product of epidermal growth factor-activated protein kinase in A-431 cell membranes, J. Biol. Chem. 255(18):8363-8365.

image.alt: AI-generated illustration: An empty vintage lab bench with a drip-stained old glass bottle beside a shiny new one and a flat glass plate.
image.caption: A lazily reused, slightly more acidic buffer pulled phosphotyrosine away from phosphothreonine; fresh buffer hid it.

audio.title: Chili peppers, a thousand liters of urine, and mice that lick their wounds
audio.transcript:
How do you measure a molecule you have never seen? And once you have caught it, how do you know what it is, or what it is for? Here are three true stories about that hunt.

Start in nineteen twelve, with Wilbur Scoville, a pharmacist at the drug company Parke, Davis in Detroit. He wanted a number for how hot a chili pepper is. He knew the burning chemical, capsaicin, but he reckoned his tongue could pick up amounts far too small for his balance to weigh. So he soaked one grain of ground pepper overnight in alcohol, then mixed that extract into sweetened water in measured proportions until the burn was weak but still there on the tongue. Japan Chillies, he found, still tasted hot at one part pepper in twenty thousand to thirty thousand. Mombasa Chillies held out to one part in a hundred thousand. He also admitted that tasting tests were frowned on in some quarters. His method became the Scoville scale, on which pure capsaicin comes in at about sixteen million. That is the logic of Rita Levi-Montalcini's halo assay. You never have to see the molecule. Your number comes from the most dilute sample the living detector still responds to.

Of course, a living detector only reports what it can feel. Stanley Cohen had already purified epidermal growth factor from mouse salivary glands, following newborn mice that opened their eyelids early, when the British biochemist Harry Gregory and his colleague Willshire went after a mystery substance in human urine. For over thirty years, people had known that urine extracts could shut down stomach acid, and the active substance had a name: urogastrone. In nineteen seventy-five, after twelve purification steps, Gregory and Willshire had less than one milligram of each pure form from every thousand liters of urine. A thousand liters. Their overall yield was three to five percent. Then Gregory worked out the sequence of the longer form, fifty-three amino acids, and laid it next to Cohen's mouse protein. Thirty-seven of the fifty-three positions matched, and the two had similar effects on stomach acid and on skin growth. Urogastrone was the human version of E G F. Two labs had chased the human and mouse versions of one growth factor through different fluids and different assays, and had given them different names.

The last story goes back to the gland where so much of this started. Why would a mouse's salivary gland be packed with nerve growth factor in the first place? Mice lick their wounds, and in the late nineteen seventies researchers found that it seems to help. Wound edges drew together faster when cage mates licked the wounds, and more slowly in mice whose salivary glands under the jaw had been removed. In nineteen eighty, a team dabbed a large form of nerve growth factor onto wounds in mice without those glands, and the edges drew together faster again. The smaller, standard form did not speed up that step. The authors were careful to say only that helping licked wounds heal may be one of the jobs of nerve growth factor in saliva. Still, it is a nice thought. The gland Cohen tried because snake venom worked too well may have been making the factor for reasons of its own.
